OdinR

Katja Danielzik (katja.danielzik@uni-due.de)

Aim of this package

High-throughput metabolic phenotyping using Odin Biolog is still relatively new in mammalian cell culture research. As such, many questions remain:

  • What do the results actually mean?
  • How do medium composition or handling affect OD readings?
  • Should cell growth be accounted for in interpretation?
  • How do we handle unexpected curve shapes?

This package aims to provide:

  • Simple reading of RawRead.csv and PlateInfo.csv files into R.
  • Noise correction: OD₅₉₀ – OD₇₄₀ (as recommended by Biolog for mammalian cells).
  • Quality control plots to spot odd or problematic OD curves.
  • Filtering of entire plates or specific curve types before analysis.
  • Calculation of Area Under the Curve (AUC) as a summary metric.
  • Normalization of AUC to the mean of control wells on the same plate.
  • Visualizations of AUC, normalized AUC, and group-level patterns.
  • Annotation of chemicals and biological metadata (e.g., KEGG pathways).
  • Heatmaps and summary plots to explore biological trends.

Important Limitations: - Not suitable for bacteria or suspension cultures — in these systems, OD₇₄₀ does reflect cell growth, so noise correction is invalid. - AUC does not capture curve dynamics — two very different curves (e.g., early peak vs. slow rise) can have the same AUC. - Does not account for cell growth — if your cells are growing rapidly, this may confound results. - Does not interpret biological meaning — a “hit” in a metabolic module does not imply pathway activation; it only means the OD was higher or lower than controls.

Important to Know Before You Start

The read_folder() function reads every RawRead.csv and PlateInfo.csv file in the specified folder and all subdirectories.

Always double-check that:

  • You’ve copied only the files you want to analyze.
  • There are no extra or duplicate files.
  • All PlateInfo.csv files have the same column order and same variable names.

Also: R is case-sensitive.
H460 ≠ h460.
0Gy ≠ 0gy.
This can cause missing data or errors later — so be careful!

Workflow

Step 1: Prepare your Data

Before you can analyze anything, you need to organize your files properly.

  1. Create a new folder (e.g., Odin_Analysis).
  2. Copy all your RawRead.csv and PlateInfo.csv files into this folder.
  3. Open each PlateInfo.csv file in Excel or a text editor.
  4. Choose one column (e.g., Description, Sample, or Well_ID) to store your experimental metadata.
  5. Enter your experimental conditions in this format:
    H460_CT_2h
    74158M4_0Gy_RMC6236_2h
    → Use underscores, no spaces, and consistent capitalization.

Why? Because read_folder() splits this column into separate variables (e.g., cell.line, condition, time.h) — and if the format is inconsistent, it will fail or create duplicates.

Step 2: Read your Data with read_folder() function

Needed user information:

  • path: the location of your folder on your machine (for windows in this format “C:”, for Linux “~/Folder)
  • variables: the order and name of your variables in your experiment
  • sample_column: the column name you stored your experiment information in (e.g H460_0Gy_RMC2363_2h) in the PlateInfo files

What follows next is the R code and the corresponding output. We included example data in this package to be able to demonstrate the workflow. Everything following a “#” in code are comments that should help understand what the code does.

library(OdinR)
data("RawRead") # load example RawRead file stored in OdinR

If you are using RStudio an object (data frame) should now be loaded to the Environment tab. You can click on it’s name to inspect the dataframe or type

head(RawRead)

Let’s look at the corresponding example PlateInfo.csv file.

data("PlateInfo") # loads PlateInfo example file from OdinR
head(PlateInfo) # shows first few rows of PlateInfo dataframe
#> # A tibble: 1 × 13
#>   PlateId  `Project Name` `Project Code` `Plate Type` Sample `Loaded At`        
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <chr>          <chr>        <chr>  <dttm>             
#> 1 0347509… Drug plates    SEA            PM-M11       H460_… 2025-11-12 09:44:07
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: `Incubation Hours` <dbl>,
#> #   `Incubation Temperature Celsius` <dbl>, `Incubated Offline` <lgl>,
#> #   `Cycle Time Minutes` <dbl>, Position <chr>, Protocol <lgl>,
#> #   Description <lgl>

In this example file the column Sample contains the experimental information.

head(PlateInfo$Sample) # shows first few rows of column storing experimental information
#> [1] "H460_CT_0Gy"

In the next I show an example code to load you data from a folder named “Odin” on drive A: and assign it to an object called data.

# data <- read_folder(data_path = "A:/Odin", # folder path
#                    sample_column = "Sample", # which column in PlateInfo contains experimental information
#                    variables = c("cell.line","condition","time.h") # sets the variable names for the following workflow)

This function does five things:

  • Read all RawRead and PlateInfo files
  • annotation (i.e. joining the information) the experimental condition from PlateInfo to RawReads
  • conduct noise correction: calculate OD at 590nm - OD at 740nm and store result in column “diff_OD_590_740”
  • create a list of dataframes that are combined in one object with elements: data containing the processed RawReads and PlateInfo files, and meta containing the provided user information about original file path, variable names and original column name containing experimental information.

Let’s load an example of multiple processed RawReads and PlateInfo files and look at the different elements:

data("processed_data") # load example output of read_folder() function

head(processed_data$data) # show first lines of element "data" in object "processed_data"
#> # A tibble: 6 × 23
#>   PlateId  `Project Name` `Project Code` `Plate Type` Sample `Loaded At`        
#>   <chr>    <chr>                   <dbl> <chr>        <chr>  <dttm>             
#> 1 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 2 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 3 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 4 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 5 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 6 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> # ℹ 17 more variables: `Incubation Hours` <dbl>,
#> #   `Incubation Temperature Celsius` <dbl>, `Incubated Offline` <lgl>,
#> #   `Cycle Time Minutes` <dbl>, Position <chr>, Protocol <lgl>,
#> #   Description <chr>, cell.line <chr>, radiation.dose <chr>, inhibitor <chr>,
#> #   time.h <chr>, `Actual Temperature Celsius` <dbl>,
#> #   `Target Temperature Celsius` <dbl>, `Read At` <dttm>, Hour <dbl>,
#> #   Well <chr>, diff_OD_590_740 <dbl>

You will find that you set variables are now not only stored in your sample_column but also separate variables. This comes in especially handy for custom analysis and visualization.

processed_data$meta  # display meta information: folder path, sample column, variables
#> $data_path
#> [1] "~/Documents/Metabolomics/odin_pipeline/data/example_data_OdinR/"
#> 
#> $sample_column
#> [1] "Description"
#> 
#> $variables
#> [1] "cell.line"      "radiation.dose" "inhibitor"      "time.h"

Now that our data is read in let’s check if we read in the data correctly.

Step3: Check your data with qc_data() function

Now that the data is in, let’s inspect it carefully.

qc_data(processed_data) # execute function qc_data() on read in data stored in object "processed_data" to create plot

This plot shows: - X-axis: First 4 wells (controls). - Y-axis: All combinations of your experimental variables. - Panels: All distinct plate types. - Color: Number of distinct OD curves per well.

What to look for:

  • One “Replicate” per well → noise correction worked.
  • No missing wells → all files were read.
  • All expected conditions → no duplicates or missing entries.
  • No grey areas → if a well is grey, it means no data was found.

If you see multiple replicates or grey wells, check:

  • Did you miss a RawRead.csv or PlateInfo.csv?
  • Is the Sample column formatted consistently?
  • Are there spaces or typos?

Step 4 (Optional): Visualize the Final Timepoint: plot_latest_timepoint()

To get a first overview we first visualize the lastest time point (i.e. end of Odin read) in 96-well format. These plots should roughly represent how your Odin plate looks like after the OD recording. In the title the specific experiment is automatically labelled and one plot is created per distinct 96-well plate in the read in data:

plot_latest_timepoint(processed_data)
#> $`74158M4_0Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M01`

#> 
#> $`74158M4_0Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M02`

#> 
#> $`74158M4_0Gy_none_2h_PM-M01`

#> 
#> $`74158M4_0Gy_none_2h_PM-M02`

#> 
#> $`74158M4_5Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M01`

#>

#> 
#> $`74158M4_5Gy_none_2h_PM-M01`

Step5: Annotate Chemicals to PlateType and Well with annotate_chemical()

To make sense of your data, you need to know what chemical is in each well.

The package includes built-in annotations for: - Metabolic plates: PM-M01, PM-M02 data(“PM_M01-M02”) - Anti-cancer drug plates: PM-M11 to PM-M14 data(“PM_M11_M14”)

data("PM_M01_M02") # load annotation file for PM-M01 and PM-M02
head(PM_M01_M02) # inspect for few rows
#> # A tibble: 6 × 11
#>   `Plate Type` Well  Chemical      `Kegg Link` Info  KEGG  module_id module_name
#>   <chr>        <chr> <chr>         <chr>       <chr> <chr> <chr>     <chr>      
#> 1 PM-M01       A01   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 2 PM-M01       A02   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 3 PM-M01       A03   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 4 PM-M01       A04   a-Cyclodextr… https://ww… C-So… C009… <NA>      <NA>       
#> 5 PM-M01       A05   Dextrin       https://ww… C-So… C007… <NA>      <NA>       
#> 6 PM-M01       A06   Glycogen      https://ww… C-So… C001… <NA>      <NA>       
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: upper_hierarchy <chr>, middle_hierarchy <chr>,
#> #   lower_hierarchy <chr>
processed_data <- annotate_chemical(processed_data, annotation = PM_M01_M02) # annotate Chemical Information
head(processed_data$data) 
#> # A tibble: 6 × 25
#>   PlateId  `Project Name` `Project Code` `Plate Type` Sample `Loaded At`        
#>   <chr>    <chr>                   <dbl> <chr>        <chr>  <dttm>             
#> 1 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 2 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 3 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 4 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 5 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> 6 c2aa34c… Julia 74158M4…            741 PM-M01       74158… 2025-05-30 13:50:36
#> # ℹ 19 more variables: `Incubation Hours` <dbl>,
#> #   `Incubation Temperature Celsius` <dbl>, `Incubated Offline` <lgl>,
#> #   `Cycle Time Minutes` <dbl>, Position <chr>, Protocol <lgl>,
#> #   Description <chr>, cell.line <chr>, radiation.dose <chr>, inhibitor <chr>,
#> #   time.h <chr>, `Actual Temperature Celsius` <dbl>,
#> #   `Target Temperature Celsius` <dbl>, `Read At` <dttm>, Hour <dbl>,
#> #   Well <chr>, diff_OD_590_740 <dbl>, Chemical <chr>, control <chr>

Now you’ll see two new columns:

  • Chemical: e.g., “Glucose”, “Lactate”, “Acetate”
  • control: “Negative Control”, “No Chemical”, “a-D-Glucose” (positive control)

If you want your annotated data at this point e.g. for further analysis with other software you can write a csv file with:

# write.csv(processed_data$data,  # just stores the dataframe but not meta information about original file path
#          file = "A:\results")  # your file path

If you want to store your complete object to keep the meta information (i.e. original folder path, …) you can store as an .RData object that only can be read by R.

# save(processed_data$data,
#     file = "A:\results")

Custom annotation files

Want to use your own plate?

  • Create a CSV with columns: Plate Type, Well, Chemical.
  • Use read_csv() and pass it to annotate_chemical().
# instal needed package
# if (!require("readr", quietly = TRUE)) {
#  install.packages("readr")
# }

# load custom annotation
# custom <- read_csv("A:/myfile.csv")
# processed_data <- annotate_chemical(processed_data, annotation = custom)

Step 6: Quality control of OD curves

In real experiments, we’ve seen: - Unexpected OD drops after an initial rise. - Wells with no increase at all. - Flat or noisy curves.

This step helps you identify and filter problematic curves.

Classify_growth_curves() adds an element classification to the our object processed_data. The classification of OD curves can be tweek with parameters. For details type ?classify_growth_curve_types in R or click on the function name and press F1, which opens the help page.

processed_data <- classify_growth_curve_types(processed_data) # classify growth curves
head(processed_data$classification)

#> $growth_curve_plots$`74158M4_5Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M01`

#> 
#> $growth_curve_plots$`74158M4_5Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M02`

#> 
#> $growth_curve_plots$`74158M4_5Gy_none_2h_PM-M01`

#> 
#> $growth_curve_plots$`74158M4_5Gy_none_2h_PM-M02`

Left panel: 96-well layout with color-coded curve types.
Right panel: Individual curves for non-growing types.

You can choose to store these plots in your “processed_data” object (for documentation) by assigning the results to your object. This creates a new element in processed_data called growth_curve_plots, in which every distinct plate is stored separately with it corresponding name compounded of the experimental variables and the plate type.

processed_data <- plot_growth_curve(processed_data) # store plots 
processed_data$growth_curve_plots$`74158M4_0Gy_RMC6236_2h_PM-M01` # just show one plot

If you make the decision to omit a complete 96-well plate (e.g. due to flat_low OD curves in the control Well, unexplainable OD drops) the function filter_data() can remove one plate from processed_data.

Let’s first recapitulate which conditions we have:

# qc_plot for overview of plate types
qc_data(processed_data)

If we made the decision that the 96-well plate with plate type “PM-M01” in cell line 74158M4, at radiation dose 0Gy and inhibitor RMC6236 and at time point 2h is not suited for further analysis we can omit this plate with:

processed_data <- filter_data(processed_data,
                              plate_type = "PM-M01",
                              filters = list(cell.line="74158M4",
                                             radiation.dose="0Gy",
                                             inhibitor="RMC6236",
                                             time.h="2h"))

We can re-use the qc_data function to check if we omitted the correct plate:

# qc_plot for overview of plate types
qc_data(processed_data)

The omitted plate has now no observations (no color).

Step 7: Summarize curves to Area under Curve (AUC)

Now that your data is clean, we can compute the AUC for each well. The compute_auc_ci() function may run for a couple seconds depending on the size of your dataset and stores the results in the element auc_results in object processed_data.

Depending on your inspection of the curve types and after potentially omitting complete plates from analysis you can decide which curve types to keep. In our example data set I demonstrate how to omit the curves with OD drops.

processed_data <- compute_auc_ci(processed_data, 
                                 target_curve_type = c("growing","flat_low","slow_growing")) # keep these curve types for AUC calculation
head(processed_data$auc_results)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 12
#>   `Plate Type` Well  cell.line radiation.dose inhibitor time.h   AUC AUC_low
#>   <chr>        <chr> <chr>     <chr>          <chr>     <chr>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 PM-M01       A01   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     11.5    11.4 
#> 2 PM-M01       A01   74158M4   5Gy            none      2h      9.61    9.57
#> 3 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     10.4    10.4 
#> 4 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   5Gy            RMC6236   2h     10.8    10.7 
#> 5 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   5Gy            none      2h     10.8    10.7 
#> 6 PM-M01       A03   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     11.3    11.2 
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: AUC_high <dbl>, n_points <int>, Chemical <chr>,
#> #   control <chr>

The AUC column contains the area under the curve. AUC_low and AUC_high are the 95% confidence intervals (from bootstrapping).

Export for external analysis:

# write.csv(processed_data$auc_results,file="A:\results")

Step 9: Check Control Well Variability wells

To get an idea about the variance of control wells (and wells containing Tween) of the same biological condition between different 96-well plates (e.g. Control wells on PM-M01 and PM-M02) we can employ the function plot_controls_tween_all_plate(). In case of anti-cancer-drug plates only the control wells are displayed. If you used custom annotation and labelled your control wells as either “Negative Control” or “No Chemical” they will be displayed here.

plot_controls_tween_all_plate(processed_data)
#> `height` was translated to `width`.

This returns a plot with:

  • x-axis: AUC per Well
  • y-axis: Control wells or wells containing Glucose or Tween, in case of anti-cancer drug plates: only control wells
  • x-axis panels: experimental conditions
  • y-axis panels: experimental conditions
  • symbol of points: type of control Well
  • color of points: Plate Type
  • dashed vertical lines: range between minimum OD of Negative Control or No Chemical over all measured wells and maximum OD

In the upper right panel in this case we can spot that the variance between control wells of different plates is higher for 0Gy 2h RMC6236 than in the other biological conditions. This is also true for variance in AUC of the Glucose Wells in this panel on PM-M01 (red squares)

Look for high variability, e.g., if 0Gy_2h_RMC6236 shows large spread, you may need to re-evaluate that condition.

If we want to get a first glimpse on how the AUCs of different biological conditions compare on the same plate we can use the plot_control_tween_per_plate() function.

plot_controls_tween_per_plate(processed_data, 
                              selected_plate = "PM-M01") # which Plate Type to compare
#> `height` was translated to `width`.

In the above plot we can e.g. see that the variance of control wells is comparably small in all biological conditions, but that the AUCs in Wells containing Glucose differr between conditions (low for none, 2h, 5Gy and high for RMC6236, 2h, 0Gy).

Step 10: Compare Controls Per Plate

After we inspected the variance of the control Wells we can proceed with visualizing all Wells on one plate type in all biological conditions:

plot_auc(processed_data, 
         selected_plate = "PM-M02",
         facet_vars = c("radiation.dose","inhibitor")) # which two biological conditions should be compared, first variable goes on y-axis panel, second on x-axis panel
#> [[1]]
#> `height` was translated to `width`.

Step 11: Normalize AUC to AUC ratios and visualize

The above visualization quickly does not scale efficiently anymore. One way to facilitate comparison of more conditions it to normalize the AUC to the mean of the control wells of the respective 96-well plate. We can do this with the function processed_data(). The results are stored in element auc_ratio results of processed_data

processed_data <- compute_auc_ratio(processed_data)
head(processed_data$auc_ratio)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 17
#>   `Plate Type` Well  cell.line radiation.dose inhibitor time.h   AUC AUC_low
#>   <chr>        <chr> <chr>     <chr>          <chr>     <chr>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 PM-M01       A01   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     11.5    11.4 
#> 2 PM-M01       A01   74158M4   5Gy            none      2h      9.61    9.57
#> 3 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     10.4    10.4 
#> 4 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   5Gy            RMC6236   2h     10.8    10.7 
#> 5 PM-M01       A02   74158M4   5Gy            none      2h     10.8    10.7 
#> 6 PM-M01       A03   74158M4   0Gy            none      2h     11.3    11.2 
#> # ℹ 9 more variables: AUC_high <dbl>, n_points <int>, Chemical <chr>,
#> #   control <chr>, mean_ctrl_AUC <dbl>, sd_ctrl_AUC <dbl>,
#> #   mean_ctrl_AUC_low <dbl>, mean_ctrl_AUC_high <dbl>, AUC_ratio <dbl>

The AUC ratios can of course be exported for to a csv file with:

# write.csv(processed_data$auc_ratio)

We can visualize the AUC ratios as a heatmap with plot_auc_ratio_heatmap(). Depending on which biological conditions you want to compare you can set the x_var argument to the variable that should be displayed on the x-axis.

plot_auc_ratio_heatmap(processed_data, 
                       plate_type = "PM-M01", # which plate type to visualize
                       x_var = "radiation.dose") # which variable should go on x-axis, all other go in x-axis panels

Missing values due to filtering or dropping of OD curve types will be displayed in grey.

In some cases, e.g. very strong signal from Glucose making distinction of other Wells impossible, it might be helpful to display the AUC ratio on the log-scale. Please not that this distorts your perception of results with higher visual emphasis on small AUC ratios compared to natural scale.

plot_auc_ratio_heatmap(processed_data, 
                       plate_type = "PM-M01", 
                       x_var = "radiation.dose",
                       scale_type = "log10" # switch from natural to log10 scale
                       )

Step 12: Annotation of metadata

If we do not only want to visualize per plate type but leverage the fact that metabolite or drugs on different plates might belong to the same group we can annotate metadata. In case of the metabolic plates PM-M01 and PM-M02 OdinR contains the annotation of metabolites to different hierarchies (module_name = pathway plus different hierarchical orders of pathways) of the KEGG database.

head(PM_M01_M02)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 11
#>   `Plate Type` Well  Chemical      `Kegg Link` Info  KEGG  module_id module_name
#>   <chr>        <chr> <chr>         <chr>       <chr> <chr> <chr>     <chr>      
#> 1 PM-M01       A01   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 2 PM-M01       A02   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 3 PM-M01       A03   Negative Con… <NA>        C-So… <NA>  <NA>      <NA>       
#> 4 PM-M01       A04   a-Cyclodextr… https://ww… C-So… C009… <NA>      <NA>       
#> 5 PM-M01       A05   Dextrin       https://ww… C-So… C007… <NA>      <NA>       
#> 6 PM-M01       A06   Glycogen      https://ww… C-So… C001… <NA>      <NA>       
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: upper_hierarchy <chr>, middle_hierarchy <chr>,
#> #   lower_hierarchy <chr>

In case of plates PM-M11 to PM-14 it contains various information from ‘Affected Pathway’ to ‘Clinical Status’.

We can annotate the metadata with:

processed_data <- annotate_metadata(processed_data, annotation = PM_M01_M02)

This adds additional columns to the element auc_ratio of processed_data, which can be exported as previously shown. In case of custom annotation you just need a dataframe with one column named Chemical and as many columns containing information on the Chemicals as needed.

Step 13: Visualiation of AUC Ratios by group

We can now group or heatmap by any column of the metadata that we find suitable. In case of many distinct entries in our chosen column it might be helpfull to only display certain entries in one specific plot. We can again choose the x-axis variable and whether we want to display the AUC ratio on the natural or log10 scale.

plot_auc_ratio_by_group(processed_data, 
                        group_var = "middle_hierarchy", # column in metadata
                        x_var = "radiation.dose",
                        group_filter = "Nucleotide metabolism") # which entries in pathway_var to display

Another summary visualization are violin plots implemented in function plot_auc_ratio_violin() which makes comparisons of AUC ratios of many groups at the same time possible. In this plot we use the information which metabolite or drug belongs to which point in the violin, but for detailed inspection the heatmaps are available.

plot_auc_ratio_violin(processed_data, 
                      pathway_var = "middle_hierarchy", 
                      color_var = "radiation.dose") # which variable should be displayed on color scale

We now have the AUC ratio on the x-axis and every point represents one metabolite/drug associated with the group on the y-axis. We can choose the variable that will be color coded and all other experimental variables are displayed in the x-axis facets. We can also again switch from natural to log-scale.

plot_auc_ratio_violin(processed_data, 
                      pathway_var = "middle_hierarchy", 
                      color_var = "inhibitor",
                      scale_type = "log10"
                      ) # which variable should be displayed on color scale
